sections.h2: Who values and who bills property in Webster County?
sections.html:
In Webster County one office sets the value and another sends the bill. Find the Assessor in Room 19 of the Marshfield courthouse, phone 417-859-2169, and the Collector down the hall in Room 15, phone 417-859-2683. Mail for the Collector goes to P.O. Box 288, Marshfield, MO 65706.

The Collector's site names Kevin Farr as the officeholder. It says the office brings in about $27 million of tax revenue each year, issues merchant licenses and conducts the delinquent tax sale every August. Counter service runs weekdays from 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. with no break for lunch.

On the valuation side, the Assessor's page defines the job as placing fair market value on property as of the tax date, with the work open to review by the county Board of Equalization and the Missouri State Tax Commission. The page links online personal property filing and a county GIS map. GIS access is a paid subscription arranged by phone.

Rates are a separate matter. Schools, cities, fire districts and the county vote on theirs, and the Taxes page of the county site posts the 2025 rates by school district.

sections.h2: When does a Webster County tax bill come due?
sections.html:
The Collector mails statements in November and treats each as due when received. After December 31 the bill is delinquent. A check mailed on or before that date needs a postmark showing it, and one postmarked later comes back unless the penalty and interest are included.

Webster County Collector rules for the tax year, as posted on the Collector's site
TopicRule
StatementsMailed in November, due upon receipt
DeadlinePostmarked December 31 to avoid penalty and interest
Missing statementContact the office if none arrives by the end of November
Older yearsDelinquent years are paid before current taxes are accepted
Mail paymentsEnclose the bottom portion of the statement
In-person paymentsBring the statement
Delinquent tax saleHeld in August

Anyone paying late follows the schedule printed on the lower part of the statement. State law treats a mailed payment as paid on its postmark date, and uses the certification date when the envelope went by registered or certified mail.

sections.h2: How are Webster County homes valued for tax?
sections.html:
Missouri taxes residences on 19 percent of market value. Marshfield's own page repeats that figure along with 32 percent for commercial and industrial property, and says the county does the assessing and collecting for the city.

New real estate values are set in odd-numbered years and stay in place the following year except for new construction. That puts the next general reset on January 1, 2027. If the Assessor wants to raise a home's value by more than 15 percent, apart from improvements, someone has to walk the property. A drive-by does not satisfy the law, and the owner has at least 30 days from the written notice to ask for an inside look.

  • Houses: 19 percent of true value.
  • Agricultural land: 12 percent.
  • Commercial and industrial: 32 percent.
  • Personal property: 33 and one-third percent, lower for livestock and farm machinery.

sections.h2: How do you contest a Webster County assessment?
sections.html:
Phone the Assessor at 417-859-2169 once a change notice lands, and ask how to set a hearing. The Board of Equalization comes first. If it keeps the number, the owner can go to the State Tax Commission, provided the appeal is filed within 30 days of the Board's final action or by the chapter's later date.

Payment need not wait. An owner who settles the whole current bill before delinquency can hand the Collector a written statement of protest, and the Collector sets aside the disputed portion in its own fund. That protest dies unless the owner sues the Collector in circuit court inside 90 days. A person with a timely Commission appeal pending skips the lawsuit, and a winning taxpayer receives the interest the fund earned.

sections.h2: Is a senior tax freeze open in Webster County?
sections.html:
The 2026 application window for the senior citizens' property tax credit ran May 1 to June 30, 2026, so it has closed. Eligible residents were 62 or older before January 1, 2026, and the credit applies to residential real estate tax on a primary residence. It holds the bill at 2026 base year levels. It is a freeze, and it does not exempt anything.

Two kinds of tax stay outside it: levies the state constitution guarantees, such as the blind fund and general obligation bonds, and voter-approved increases adopted after the base year. Vehicle tax and other personal property tax are excluded too. Applicants went to the County Clerk's office in Room 12 with photo identification, a utility bill or voter card as proof of residency, and the paid 2025 receipt. The Clerk's line is 417-859-8683. Ask when the next window opens and what a mid-year sale does to an approved freeze.

sections.h2: What does the Marshfield city levy add to a bill?
sections.html:
Marshfield property owners pay the city's levy on top of the school, county and special district rates. After voters approve general obligation bonds, the Board of Aldermen sets a debt service rate high enough to cover principal and interest. The parks and cemetery levy has a ceiling that only voters can lift. That ceiling lets collections rise by 5 percent or the Consumer Price Index, whichever is lower, against the prior year.

The county Taxes page breaks its 2025 rate tables into Diggins, Fordland, Marshfield, Niangua, Rogersville, Seymour and Strafford school districts, plus rural Webster County. Match the district printed on your statement, not the mailing city.

sections.h2: How do you pay a Webster County bill?
sections.html:
• At the Collector's counter, with the statement in hand.
  • By mail, with the bottom portion of the statement enclosed.
  • On the Collector's website by e-check, debit or credit card, where cards add a convenience fee.
  • Cash, personal check, money order or cashier's check, and one check may cover several bills.

The Collector says it is not responsible if you pay tax on property that belongs to someone else or skip a parcel you own, so check the account number against your parcel. A statement that never reached you does not erase the tax, penalty or interest.

sections.h2: What do Census figures say about Webster County households?
sections.html:
Webster County counted 36,202 people in the 2010 census and 39,085 in 2020. The 2020 to 2024 survey shows 13,964 households, and 87.6 percent of residents were in the same house one year earlier. The county is home to 2,990 veterans.

Owners occupy 77.4 percent of occupied homes, the lowest share of Stone, Warren and Webster, so renters have a larger presence here. Landlords get their statements in November like other owners and face the same December 31 postmark date.

The county sits in the Springfield metropolitan area. Its cities are Fordland, Marshfield, Niangua, Rogersville, Seymour and Strafford, and Diggins is the lone village. Marshfield, the seat, stands at 1,490 feet, the highest county seat in the state, and a Carthage marble courthouse built from 1939 to 1941 anchors the square.

faqs.q: When do Webster County property taxes become delinquent?
faqs.a: After December 31. Statements are due once received, and a mailed check needs a postmark by that date.

faqs.q: Where is the Webster County Collector located?
faqs.a: Room 15 of the courthouse, 101 S. Crittenden Street, Marshfield. Mail goes to P.O. Box 288, and the phone is 417-859-2683.

faqs.q: Can I pay a Webster County bill by card?
faqs.a: Yes, online or at the office, and debit or credit cards carry a convenience fee. E-check is also offered.

faqs.q: Is the Webster County senior freeze accepting applications?
faqs.a: Not now. The 2026 window ended June 30, 2026. The County Clerk at 417-859-8683 can say when the next opens.

faqs.q: Who decides Webster County tax rates?
faqs.a: Each taxing body does, meaning schools, cities, fire districts and the county. The Assessor and Collector do not.
